statement: Most verbs have six inflectional forms: three primary (preterite, 3rd singular present, plain present) and three secondary (plain form, gerund-participle, past participle).
condition: Applies to the inflectional paradigm of an ordinary (non-be) verb lexeme: primary forms are preterite, 3rd person singular present tense and plain present tense; secondary forms are the plain form, the gerund-participle and the past participle.

correct.text: I need to write it. [plain form]

statement: The verb be has two preterite forms (was, were) and three present forms (am, is, are); irrealis 'were' is a residual mood form found only with be and a 1st or 3rd person singular subject.
condition: Applies to the verb be: preterite was/were, present am/is/are; irrealis mood 'were' (as in 'I wish she were here') occurs only with be with a 1st or 3rd person singular subject.

correct.text: I wish she were here. [irrealis were]

concept: case forms of pronouns and nouns
statement: A few pronouns have four case forms (we, us, our, ours); most nouns contrast only genitive and plain case, case is determined by the NP's function, and genitive is marked on the last word of the NP (head genitive or phrasal genitive).
condition: Applies to case marking: nominative, accusative, dependent genitive and independent genitive for a few pronouns; plain vs genitive (dog vs dog's, dogs vs dogs') for most nouns; genitive marking falls on the last word, usually the head noun but sometimes on the last word of a post-head dependent.

statement: Auxiliaries have additional negative primary forms, whereas lexical verbs do not have corresponding negative inflectional forms.
condition: When a verb lexeme is lexical rather than auxiliary, its primary verb form (including a preterite or present-tense form) cannot itself bear the auxiliary negative form -n't.
violation: A negative -n't form is created by attaching -n't directly to a lexical verb form, such as a lexical preterite or third-person-singular present form.

correct.text: The driver doesn't stop at the crossing.

concept: absence of secondary forms in modal auxiliaries
statement: Modal auxiliaries lack all secondary verb forms: the plain form, gerund-participle, and past participle.
condition: When a modal auxiliary is required in a position selecting a secondary verb form—after infinitival to, in a gerund-participial construction, or after perfect have—the modal auxiliary has no form that can fill that position.
violation: A modal auxiliary is used as though it had a plain form after infinitival to, a gerund-participle form with -ing, or a past participle after perfect have.

concept: invariant present form of modal auxiliaries
statement: A modal auxiliary has one present-tense form for subjects of every person and number; it does not take a third-person-singular -s form.
condition: When a modal auxiliary is the finite verb in a present-tense clause, its form remains the same with first-, second-, and third-person singular and plural subjects.
violation: A present-tense modal auxiliary is given a third-person-singular -s suffix.
